item.title: What Jumping to Conclusions Reveals About Your Wounds
item.description:
Anxiety

What Jumping to Conclusions Reveals About Your Wounds

What feels like insight is actually a mirror.

Posted September 7, 2026

Key points
  • In moments of uncertainty, you create a story to explain someone else's behavior. That story is rarely true.
  • The story reflects your own vulnerability and past wounds, not the other person's intentions.
  • Noticing the story, rather than believing it, allows you to respond wisely.

When Lisa sends an email or text and it is not quickly responded to, she worries that the person is mad at her.

When Tim’s employee responds to a request with pushback, he feels that he is being taken advantage of by his employee and builds a case to support this belief.

When Yvonne’s manager is not available to help her solve a problem, she feels disrespected and undervalued.

The story each tells themselves reveals not a truth about the other person, but a vulnerability and wound within themselves.

There is an often underappreciated human tendency; something we all do when in emotionally charged situations. Into the space of the unknown — whether it is the reason someone is doing something, what they are feeling, or what they are thinking — we will create a story to eliminate uncertainty. That story, more so than the facts, is what fuels our anxiety and distress. And this part is important: That story is rarely true.

While the story rarely matches what the other person is thinking or doing, or what is motivating their behavior, it does reveal something important about ourselves. It points us to a core relational wound or our greatest emotional fear, which then becomes our default expectation.

Think about this for yourself. Reflect on moments of emotional distress in circumstances lacking certainty. Most likely, you have a set, default assumption — a story to explain someone else’s behavior that you return to time and again in different situations and with different people. The common denominators are uncertainty and your particular flavor of vulnerability.

These stories are often born from an unmet need, a hurtful dynamic within our family of origin or peers, or a core vulnerability we carry from childhood or repeated adult experiences. If you felt overlooked within your family of origin, you may impose a story of not being valued any time someone else’s behavior feels dismissive or uninterested. If you question your value and worth, you may impose a story of rejection onto someone else’s behavior that doesn’t match your hoped-for response. If you felt overpowered or controlled as a child, you may project a story of another's intent to manipulate you when their actions don’t align with your expectations. The story generally matches a wound. In the words of couples therapist Terry Real, “Show me the thumbprint, and I’ll tell you about the thumb.”

This story is typically an attempt to protect yourself from being hurt or harmed in a way that feels familiar and expected. As is often true with other self-protective mechanisms, when it becomes overgeneralized and applied in all situations, not just the ones that created it in the first place, it may create more harm than help.

Because this is a human tendency, you won’t stop the story from arriving in emotionally charged moments. But you can notice when it arrives and choose a different response. Here’s how.

  1. Notice when you are imposing a story into the unknown. A clue will be the presence of emotional distress and, perhaps, rumination or dwelling.
  2. Ask yourself what you actually know to be true. What are the facts?
  3. Identify the story. This will involve the intentions, motivations, thoughts, and feelings you are assigning to someone else in the absence of knowing.
  4. Recognize that the story reflects your own vulnerability, not the other person’s truth.
  5. Show yourself compassion for carrying the story.
  6. Remember the story is most likely not true right now, unless you have specific experience with this person that supports it.
  7. Move forward from who you want to be in this moment, not from the wound.
  8. Notice what happens. What actually happened? How did the other person respond?
article continues after advertisement

This is the practice that helps to build new experiences, which build a cushion around the hurt parts of yourself, so that they feel softened and protected.

item.title: I Didn't Want to Be a Burden. AI Never Made Me Feel Like One
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

I Didn't Want to Be a Burden. AI Never Made Me Feel Like One

Personal Perspective: Life with AI is better, but what is it doing to my brain?

Posted September 7, 2026

Key points
  • For years, I avoided burdening others with unfinished thinking, so I stopped thinking out loud entirely.
  • AI became the thinking partner I never had, and my writing and businesses have improved because of it.
  • Research links heavy AI reliance to measurable declines in independent problem-solving ability.
  • Two guardrails, self-awareness and directed engagement, keep AI from replacing my own thinking.

I've always thought better out loud, in conversation, bouncing an idea off someone until it sharpens.

But I rarely do that.

I have always worried about burdening other people, and asking them to listen to me while I brainstorm ideas has always felt exactly like that. There's a cost to asking someone to sit with your unfinished thinking, listening to you ramble, while you try to figure out what's really happening inside your head.

I mostly decided it wasn't fair to ask. And my thinking was restrained, without even being aware of it.

Over the last couple of years, I've begun to work with AI pretty intensely every day: writing, planning, thinking through problems in my businesses, mapping outreach initiatives, working out ideas before they're ready to say out loud.

It has changed how I work.

How is AI impacting my brain?
Source: Turgay Koca / Pexels

A Different Kind of Burden

But I've become genuinely concerned about what AI is doing to my brain even though I continue to use it for hours most days. The research on the cognitive impacts of AI use has been trickling in, and it isn't reassuring.

There are some disturbing terms being coined around our brain on AI. Shaw and Nave (2026) coined "Cognitive Surrender," and Kosmyna et al. (2026) coined "Cognitive Debt," which doesn't feel any better. The more a tool does your thinking for you, the less practice your brain gets doing it on its own. Liu and colleagues (2026) found that after just 10 minutes of AI-assisted problem-solving, people did significantly worse once they no longer had access to AI.

And I still start most mornings by opening AI.

I have noticed it is much harder for me to start with a blank page when I can just interact with AI to get started. I don't even bother trying to write marketing copy anymore and instead outsource it to AI. I feel a growing reluctance to do the nitty-gritty work that makes ideas real.

I have found myself mentally calculating the risks and rewards of using AI.

The Thinking Partner I Never Had

While there are real risks, I feel free to think with AI in ways I never have with anyone before. AI isn't a person I'm taking time from. So I ask it everything, and for the first time I have a thinking partner I can use as often as I need, and that need only seems to grow.

article continues after advertisement

That's the trap and the bonus at the same time. I go deeper into my own ideas with AI than I ever did alone. My writing has improved. My businesses have moved further in the last year than anything I've tried in the past. I'm building the lifestyle I've always wanted, one that's better for my physical and mental health. Even concepts I've been developing for more than two decades have become deeper and better articulated through exploring them with AI.

They are still my ideas, but stronger and more useful for others.

The Cost of Not Having to Start

But the more I lean on that partnership, the less I reach for solitary thought at all, because I've gotten used to not having to start by myself.

Over the past two years of thinking about and working with AI this closely, I've built a framework for using it safely and effectively: the AI Awareness Arc. In it, I've developed two crucial approaches for interacting with AI: self-awareness and directed engagement. Those two approaches are what keep me intentional with every AI interaction, and intentional use is what guards against the cognitive risks.

I decide what I'm trying to get out of an interaction before I start, and I stop when I've gotten it, instead of drifting through a chat with no endpoint. And, maybe most importantly, I established a rule that requires AI to ask me questions rather than just hand me answers.

This piece is an example. I sat down with AI knowing only that I wanted to write about my AI use, but from a different perspective. Instead of asking AI what to write about, I told it to ask me questions. By the third or fourth question, it became clear to me what was percolating in my mind: how AI was impacting my own brain. The questions took me from a small kernel to a full concept, and it was more fun than doing it alone would have been.

It sounds like a small thing, but it changes what my brain is doing while I work. Answering a question is active, and so is brainstorming. Receiving a finished conclusion or document without that process is passive, and passive is where the real risk of offloading to AI lives.

Risk Versus Reward, Ongoing

There's research on what causes cognitive risk and almost none on what prevents it. What I have is a practice, and it's more cumbersome and less satisfying than letting AI hand me the answer.

I never wanted to burden anyone with my unfinished thinking, and working with AI solved that. It also means I've gone two years without asking a single person to sit with an idea while I worked it out. I haven't gotten better at asking.

article continues after advertisement

I'm building ideas better, but not asking people to listen to what I'm thinking. My life is better, but I worry more about my brain. Self-awareness and directed engagement are my guardrails. They'll tell me when my thinking partner has quietly become my brain.

item.title: My Great Expectations and the Pursuit of Worth
item.description:
Ethics and Morality

My Great Expectations and the Pursuit of Worth

Personal Perspective: We all need worthy work, but not at the expense of others.

Posted September 7, 2026

I have recently reread two of Dickens' best books: Great Expectations and Bleak House. Both are brilliant books about wanting the wrong things from life, or hunting what we want in the wrong places. In "Great Expectations," Pip, the hero or the antihero, believes Miss Havisham, a wealthy spinster who is disappointed in love, has bestowed a fortune on him; and in "Bleak House," Richard, the Jarndyce ward, bankrupts himself and his wife Ada and ultimately destroys himself in his efforts to win an endless and futile legal case. Pip learns that the money he believed came from Miss Havisham was really from a convict whom he had helped in his youth, and Richard ends up in debt and ultimately destroyed by his futile efforts to win the case. Pip, in his fruitless search to be a fine gentleman, leaves behind the people who really love him: Joe Gargery and Biddy. And Richard spurns the good Mr Jarndyce, who supports him and only wants the best for him in life.

Reading these wise and wonderful books, I asked myself if my own expectations and aims, my struggles in the literary world, were in vain and ultimately an endless source of effort for no worthy reward. I wonder if I neglected and even exposed my family or old friends, being caught up in the competition to win fame and fortune. Or if it was important to reach a large audience with my words, to publish yet another book, or even a short story in a publication when someone dear to me might desperately need my help.

The Necessity for Worthy Work

Of course, we need to establish our independence and find work and worthy endeavors to sustain us through our lives. But we can consider the cost of our ambitions and efforts. Dickens, for example, has several women, including Mrs Jellyby in Bleak House, bent on helping people in faraway Nigeria. At home, she makes her daughter Caroline work as her secretary, and she is less worried about her many small children falling down the stairs or almost starving.

When we look at our lives and work goals, some people are driven by greed, money, and fame, or by the desire to succeed more than a rival. But we can try to live a meaningful life, help those around us in need, and above all, help those nearest and dearest; people who love us and whom we love.

Source: Madonna and Child with Saint Elizabeth and Saint John the Baptist, Jacopino del Conte, circa 1535

item.title: Why Your Greatest Strength Is Your Biggest Problem
item.description:
Cognitive Reappraisal

Why Your Greatest Strength Is Your Biggest Problem

The psychology of why your best qualities are the ones most likely to trap you.

Posted September 7, 2026

Key points
  • Psychologist Diana Hill's "genius energy" framework reveals how our core strengths become failure modes.
  • The Einstellung effect shows that known solutions physically block our ability to perceive better ones.
  • Curiosity, not harder effort, is the mechanism that loosens the grip of cognitive entrenchment.

In psychologist Diana Hill's new book Wise Effort, she provides a striking image: A bird flies into her kitchen through an open door, panics, and heads straight for the large window, mistaking it for the way out. It slams into the glass, tumbles to the floor, gathers itself, and tries again — harder this time, and with even more urgency.

Hill writes: "It's so relatable, isn't it? We are going about our lives, doing our thing, and then find ourselves stuck. And we do the exact same thing those birds do. We think if we just fly harder, go faster, or push ourselves more, we will get out."

The bird has effort in abundance, but that effort is working against its own aims. It's a perfect metaphor for human striving. Anyone who has watched a talented person grind themselves into dust doing the thing they're best at has seen the human version of this exact phenomenon. How can we orient ourselves differently to our goals? How do we exert effort that works with our aims?

The Genius Trap

Each of has a unique, idiosyncratic combination of strenghts, which Hill calls our "genius energy". Here, she's drawing on the word's Roman roots, where a genius was a guardian spirit believed to watch over a person or family. Your genius, as Hill describes, is the combination of personality, talents, interests, character strengths, and emotional intelligence that makes you distinctively you. It's the persistence that built your career, and the emotional sensitivity that makes you the friend everyone calls at midnight.

Cognitive entrenchment can result from rigid thinking
Source: yogendra singh via UnSplash

Hill's central argument here is that your genius energy, the force that fuels your best work and deepest relationships, is also the thing most likely to wreck you when it's overused or pointed in the wrong direction. This is you as a bird, stuck in the kitchen, repeatedly hitting its beak against the glass. Your greatest strength contains your most reliable, and most predictable, mode of failure.

Robert Kaplan and Robert Kaiser, working in organizational psychology, have shown that leadership strengths follow a curvilinear pattern: Decisiveness is an asset until it becomes bulldozing, and empathy serves you beautifully until it curdles into conflict avoidance. Most leaders, they found, have essentially no awareness of where that line is. They just keep doing more of what got them promoted.

The cognitive psychologist Erik Dane has a term for the deeper mechanism at work here: cognitive entrenchment. The more expertise you develop in a domain, the more rigid your mental schemas become. You get faster and more efficient, yes, but you also lose the ability to see solutions that fall outside your established patterns. Chess masters, paradoxically, can be slower than intermediate players at solving problems that require unconventional moves. Expertise builds walls around your thinking.

article continues after advertisement

There's an even more specific version of this called the Einstellung effect, and it's one of those findings that feels like it should be printed on coffee mugs and distributed to every ambitious person on the planet. When people already know one solution to a problem, that known solution literally blocks them from perceiving a better one. Eye-tracking studies have shown that participants' gaze physically gravitates toward the familiar answer, even when a superior alternative is sitting right there.

The Three Traps

Hill organizes the ways genius goes sideways into a few patterns, and in a recent conversation, she put it with characteristic directness: "Am I stuck in a story? Am I holding too tight to something? Or am I running away from discomfort? Those questions, plopping them into any situation, can be really helpful."

Hill walked away from an ultra-successful podcast
Source: will francis via UnSplash

Hill knows this experience personally. In 2021, Hill was cohosting a wildly successful psychology podcast. It had nearly two million downloads, and was on the verge of lucrative sponsorships. Everything looked perfect from the outside.

And she wanted out. She longed to explore ideas that sat at the edges of psychology and spirituality, but her genius for persistence, the very quality that had built her career, kept her locked in. She started having panic attacks before team meetings. Her body was screaming for change while her mind recited the old script: push through the glass, fly harder.

The Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT) research tradition that Hill draws from calls what she eventually did "psychological flexibility," and it turns out to be one of the most robust predictors of mental health and well-being across hundreds of studies. This is the capacity to shift one's strategy based on what the current moment actually requires, rather than defaulting to whatever worked last time.

Tasting the Strawberry Again

Tasting the strawberry, a new, proves a compelling metaphor for curiosity
Source: josh withers via UnSplash

So what, then, loosens the grip? In a recent conversation, Hill kept returning to curiosity. She makes a crucial distinction between two primary forms. There's deprivation curiosity: the itch to find the answer, look it up, and close the loop. And then there's interest curiosity: the kind that leads to more questions, that finds the not-knowing itself to be generative.

article continues after advertisement

Hill makes the case that we can enter into a mode of interest curiosity with more ease than we realize. "If you taste a strawberry, you think you already know what a strawberry tastes like. But if you were truly curious, every one of those strawberries would be a completely different experience. We assume we already know. Imagine if you entered a work meeting like that."

This is one of the ways in which we can relinquish ourselves from the genius trap. Get curious about what's at hand, and become curious about whether the thing you're best at is actually what this moment requires.

item.title: Dangerous Books and Why Vice Is a Virtue in Literature
item.description:
Ethics and Morality

Dangerous Books and Why Vice Is a Virtue in Literature

Literature uses fiction to depict truth and vice to reveal virtue.

Posted September 7, 2026

Key points
  • In recent years, the calls for censorship and banning books has increased.
  • Critiques of the dangerous or immoral nature of literature have been around for thousands of years.
  • Yet one of literature's great strengths is to depict the complexity of the human condition.
  • Showing truth through fiction and revealing virtue by depicting vice, literature helps us to mature ethically.
Source: Unsplash / Jason Leung

“It's a mistake to conflate the author with his characters. Characters exist to perfect the author; both his virtues and his vices.”—Jean-Luc Beauchard, The Fruit of Death

For more than 400 years, the Catholic Church maintained the Index Librorum Prohibitorum, a list of books deemed morally dubious, if not outright dangerous, by the Sacred Congregation of the Index and thus banned from being printed and read by the faithful. While many of the titles contained therein advanced positions explicitly contrary to the Church’s teachings, others portrayed vicious characters acting viciously.

Taking a page from Plato’s Republic, which warns of the corrupting influence of the poetic arts, the Sacred Congregation's work was motivated by the fear that impressionable readers may imitate the sinful behavior depicted in works of fiction. If reading books on chivalry can convince Don Quixote that he is a knight, the thinking went, what prevents the reader of Stendhal or Flaubert from entering into a torrid love affair?

Such thinking may seem puritanical and out-of-date, but worries over the shaping influence literature has on human desire are as alive today as they were during the Middle Ages. Not only are there calls for censorship from both sides of the political aisle, but even the way contemporary readers tend to evaluate literary merit evinces a kind of crude moralism that appraises a work solely on whether it affirms the reader’s previously held convictions.

How often does an assessment of a given work depend on whether or not the reader liked the main character? How many reviews criticise a novel for depicting objectionable people who espouse vile ideologies and participate in morally bankrupt behavior? Alternatively, how many of the most celebrated and award-winning books present the right kinds of people doing the right kinds of things, suggesting that, yes, the author and the reader too are good people and thus ought to feel good about seeing their virtues represented on the page?

The Limits of Moral Evaluation

Part of the problem is that this flattening of literature’s horizon to narrowly moral (and moralizing) categories actually diminishes its moral force. One of the great advantages a work of fiction has over, say, a philosophical treatise is that it can present various perspectives and lifestyles alongside one another and invite readers to decide for themselves which, if any, is worth pursuing.

article continues after advertisement

Such approaches risk confusing fiction’s aim—which ought to be to give a true accounting of life’s richness and complexity through artificial creation—with the goals of the childhood fable. Not every story is meant to make readers good, though every compelling story presents us with characters who must choose either for or against what is good. And this is the brilliance of literature: It uses fiction to tell the truth and teaches virtue through vice.

Source: Unsplash /Matias North

An example from one of my favorite books: The Kafkaesque novella Michael Kohlhaas by Heinrich von Kleist is about an honest horse trader who is treated dishonestly. Lied to, abused, and dispossessed of his horses by his menacing neighbor, the Junker Wenzel von Tronka, Kohlhaas starts by seeking justice through the legitimate authorities.

How a Character Can Embody Ethical Ambiguity

His adversary is incredibly well-connected; the pious tradesman begins to fear that his pleas will fall on deaf ears. What does he do? In a manner reminiscent of every Jason Statham movie ever made, he takes matters into his own hands. Raising a rebel army, burning and pillaging villages, and hunting the Junker across the countryside, Kohlhaas sets out to satisfy his thirst for justice by whatever means necessary, and many unnecessary means besides.

I won’t spoil one of the most darkly comic books I have ever read, but I often think of Kohlhaas when my own desire for justice flares up. How far am I willing to go to see to it that that desire is met? Will I, like Kohlhaas, declare, “May God never forgive me as I mean to forgive the Junker?" Or will I step back for my passion to abate, seeing that the more I insist upon the justice of my cause, the more unjust I run the risk of becoming? Will I fight with bitterness and bile or seek a less destructive, though potentially less satisfying outcome?

Aristotle wrote of the necessity of finding moral exemplars to whom we can look for mentorship and guidance as we progress along the path toward maturity and ethical development. What good literature offers is not only moral exemplars but immoral ones; or, better, real human beings who possess all of the strengths and flaws, virtues and vices, and especially the messiness of real people in real situations.

article continues after advertisement

To some, this may make such characters problematic and the books in which they reside immoral and even dangerous. But to those of us who respect good readers enough to trust that they will not simply imitate whatever they find depicted on the page, it makes such characters indispensable. After all, how impoverished would our world be without them?

Source: Unsplash / Thought Catalog

item.title: Preparing for High-Stress Training Evolutions
item.description:
Self-Talk

Preparing for High-Stress Training Evolutions

Practice for the pressure.

Posted September 7, 2026

Key points
  • Visualization using all five senses can boost performance and ease anxiety during simulations.
  • Performance breathing, like box or diaphragmatic breathing, quickly manages physiological stress.
  • Adaptive self-talk and cognitive reframing counteract negative thoughts and improve outcomes.

During underwater egress training, aka helicopter dunker training, one of my fellow students panicked and stopped the training so that he could get out. This training teaches key survival skills for aviation personnel flying in helicopters over water. It involves being harnessed into a seat in a mock helicopter, which then “crashes” into a pool, sinks, and inverts. You are required to follow precise instructions in order to save yourself. Pretty much everyone experiences anxiety during the training.

The interesting thing about this training is that it doesn’t require much swimming ability or any advanced technical skills. What it does require is mental control during a time in which you are anxious and disoriented (upside down, underwater, with ineffective vision and hearing, and without air). The goal is to manage your anxiety during the evolution, while learning that you are capable of saving yourself despite the anxiety. The training builds skills, normalizes the stress, and instills confidence that you can do it in a real situation.

You might be wondering what happened to my classmate? He was referred to the mental health department to help him with his anxiety. The problem was that he didn’t have a mental health disorder, and meeting with the mental health provider didn’t help him. In a small-world story, he ended up in my office. He learned visualization, performance breathing, the power of self-talk, cognitive reframing, and, through gradual exposure and practice of his new mental skills, he crushed the dunker.

These mental skills are integral for personnel undergoing high-risk training evolutions. Mental preparation for the training required in public safety positions is critical. It transfers to real-life scenarios, and many of the techniques are tied to long-term health. Realism and anxiety are necessary components of these trainings, be they fire-fighting training, survival training, flight training, or law enforcement, correctional, or military scenarios.

Preparing for high-stress and high-risk training evolutions requires a number of mental skills. These skills are necessary for those making rapid, high-stakes decisions.
Source: Image by ThePixelman from Pixabay

The following are important mental skills which improve training performance.

Training/Technical-Related Knowledge and Skills

Though it should go without saying, knowing the educational material related to the training in question (e.g., live fire exercise) and practicing the skills to the extent that you can prior to the event are necessary. We all know that if you haven’t studied for the test, you have almost no chance of doing well on the test. Mastering the technical material will make everything else easier and help you gain confidence faster.

Visualization

To help with mastering the material, performing optimally, and decreasing stress during the event, visualization is key. For visualization (also called imagery and mental practice) to be most effective, do the following: Use a first-person perspective (i.e., view it as you will during the event, not as though you are observing yourself); include every detail of the upcoming training event possible to include all necessary steps involved in the task; engage all five senses and imagine the associated sights, sounds, smells, touch, necessary movements, and emotions. Mental rehearsal can be used for emergency scenarios, to improve decision making under stress, or to practice multiple outcomes or scenarios which may be presented during any given training event.

article continues after advertisement

Performance Breathing

Deep breathing is the fastest way to achieve physiological control, slowing down heart rate, regulating breath rate, and facilitating the management of anxiety. For this to work on demand, practice is important between and during training events. In addition to practicing such techniques as box breathing (breath in for 4 counts, hold for 4 counts, exhale for 4 counts and hold again for 4 counts – repeat) or diaphragmatic breathing (e.g., belly breathing), yoga and meditation allow for more advanced breathing practice and control. Mindfulness meditation in particular has been shown to alter time perception, literally providing individuals the sense that time has slowed. This type of mental control can be incredibly valuable when needing to make rapid, high stakes decisions.

Self-Talk

Self-talk can be instructional or motivational. In instructional self-talk, you provide yourself task-specific instructions related to the task at hand. In motivational self-talk you provide yourself motivation and instill confidence (e.g., I’ve got this!). Both improve our performance during challenging tasks. It is notable that negative and defeatist self-talk can sabotage our efforts.

Cognitive Reframing

Being aware of our thoughts in the moment (believe it or not this takes practice!) allows us to examine them and re-interpret or change them to thoughts which are more adaptive, realistic, and healthy. As an example, imagine you are a student who enters into a high risk training evolution and experiences an increased heart rate, based on the thought, “I’m going to fail this event.” This thought is an example of all-or-nothing thinking and an avoidance of knowledge of the very real obstacles that you’ve already successfully faced to advance to that particular point in training. This kind of thought will interfere with event performance. To manage it, ask yourself, is this thought supported by any evidence? What would I tell a friend in this situation who was having this thought? Finally, reframe the thought to something like, “I have prepared for this; it’s normal to be nervous; I can do this.”

Embrace Critical Feedback

Training programs are the places where we are expected to make mistakes, and in high-risk situations, you want any mistakes to occur in the training environment where there are safety measures in place. Often, how you respond to critical feedback in these training sessions is more important to the training program than the mistake you made. Reviewers want to see that you are able to think about your own performance objectively, are open to feedback, and are able to adapt and adjust your technique or approach. These skills provide a definite edge in training and beyond.

article continues after advertisement

Mental skills are as important to master as the technical skills needed for any high risk training. The beauty of mental skills is that they readily transfer to other areas of our lives. Incorporating them into your daily battle rhythm will have immediate and long term effects across your career.

item.title: How Going Deeper Can Lead to a Richer Life
item.description:
Relationships

How Going Deeper Can Lead to a Richer Life

Personal Perspective: Why do we rush? Staying longer with what is already here.

Posted September 7, 2026

During the COVID pandemic, life changed in many ways for all of us. We are still finding the effects of this scary and totally unusual time in our lives. While most pandemic stories were sad and filled with loss, just as many wonderful, inspiring, and significant stories changed lives and how we look at life.

I have a story from that time that has had a major impact on my view of life; it also came with corresponding practical actions. We can then apply the key learning from that story to a question that I have had and continue to grapple with in my life. “What if the life we are seeking is not somewhere else, but deeper inside the life we already have and are experiencing currently?

For me, the pandemic held a great risk, as I have a blood disease that lowers my immune response. We were all hearing stories of people with compromised immune systems dying from the COVID virus. This meant that our family sheltered in place and, when possible, we spent time outside with family and friends.

Source: Julia Cameron / Pexels

A few months into the COVID pandemic, my partner Teresa and I decided to form a pod of four with another couple, who live near us in the northeastern corner of Connecticut. Within several months of dinner and lively, deep conversations, four to five times a week, we all noticed profound changes in our 20-year relationship. We each noticed changes in ourselves, and we noticed that our relationship as two couples changed. We became more open and trusting, laughed more, and most of all, had deeper, more meaningful discussions on many topics. I started perceiving aspects of our relationship and each person in ways that were very new and different. I found myself more open, inquisitive, interested, accepting, trusting, and most of all, more loving with the “COVID pod members of northwest Connecticut.”

This experience inspired me to dig deeper into how sustained, deeper attention to relationships, questions, experiences, and parts of ourselves reveals more when we are with them a moment longer, instead of rushing on to the next thing or a quick resolution. The four of us were together so often that it created something magical in the group and in each of us.

I challenge you to contrast this deepening with the more familiar modern-day experience: finishing or skimming an article or book before absorbing it, reaching for the phone during planned silence, changing subjects when a conversation becomes vulnerable, or looking for the next experience before inhabiting the present one. The essential tension is that we often equate growth with novelty and change. Might it be more likely that the most important things reveal themselves more through the willingness to be present and go deeper? “To linger a bit longer” than we normally feel comfortable?

Here are some other examples: When a conversation approaches vulnerability, we redirect it. When grief begins to surface, we become busy. When a recurring pattern becomes more visible, we tend to explain it away. And lastly, when a relationship beckons us to change, we retreat to the familiar. Many of us are dependent on things like our phone, work, or TV time. From this lens, they are less conscious and move us more horizontally than vertically and deeper in our lives.

With the vast amount of information available, we are dependent and we want more; correspondingly, we have fewer opportunities for depth of meaning or deeper conversations. In addition, authentic curiosity and authentic conversation are harder and take more courage and discipline. Decisions are easier when you can make them through a narrower perspective, but danger comes when we make those decisions through the lens of bias; most of the time, we confirm our biases. All of this points to a vastly more transaction-based society where we no longer deepen our thinking or conversations; we push down emotions and push toward quick resolutions.

Staying five minutes longer is a simple practice. Choose one conversation, feeling, question, or experience. When you feel the impulse to move on, stay five minutes longer, and ask yourself: What becomes visible only because I stayed and made myself more available to the depth of the moment?

The following is a series of questions that we can reconsider in our lives.

  • What if the life that you are seeking is already here and available and you just aren’t seeing it?

  • What is the difference and the impact between moving on and going deeper?

  • What would it take for me to stop searching for more and start going deeper?

  • What if I asked one more question even when I felt like I knew the answer?

Let me conclude with a tie-back to the story about our friends who we sheltered in place with during the pandemic. Years later, it is even more evident that we transformed our relationship by going deeper and staying longer during that time. Our relationships have been literally transformed, and I am very pleased to say that I am, and we are, staying longer and going deeper with many others in our lives.

There is an alternative to always searching outside of ourselves that may lead us to the following. What if we stay and not search for the next thing? By cultivating the practice of deepening, you could find a richer life experience.
